title: Daily Temperatures
description: Brute force to optimized: a forward scan per day versus a monotonic decreasing stack of indices that resolves every day's wait at once.

blocks.text: Given an array of integers temperatures representing daily temperatures, return an array answer such that answer[i] is the number of days you would have to wait after day i to see a STRICTLY WARMER temperature. If there is no future day with a warmer temperature, answer[i] should be 0.

blocks.caption: A monotonic decreasing stack of day-indices resolves every day's "wait for warmth" in a single linear pass

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An array of daily temperatures"],["Output","An array where each entry is the number of days until a warmer temperature, or 0 if none exists"],["Goal","Find every day's \"wait\" in a single linear pass"],["Constraints","1 <= temperatures.length <= 10^5; 30 <= temperatures[i] <= 100"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Number of days until the next WARMER (larger) value\" for every position","The classic monotonic decreasing stack technique (structurally identical to Next Greater Element I)"],["The answer is a DAY COUNT (index difference), not the warmer temperature itself","Once the warmer day is found (via the stack), the answer is simply the current index MINUS the waiting day's index"]]}

blocks.text: This is the "next greater element" pattern, but instead of returning the next larger VALUE, it asks for the number of days (the index gap) until that next larger value appears.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting How Many Days Until the Weather Finally Warms Up
blocks.text: Imagine tracking daily temperatures and, for each day, wanting to know exactly how many days pass before the FIRST warmer day arrives. Walking through the days while keeping track of which earlier days are still "waiting" for warmth: the moment a warmer day appears, it immediately resolves the wait for every earlier day it is warmer than, and that wait is simply the gap in day-numbers between them.

blocks.caption: The stack holds day-indices still waiting for warmth; a warmer day resolves the wait for every cooler day currently waiting on top

blocks.content: {"headers":["Day (temp)","Wait","Why"],"rows":[["Day 0 (73)","1","Day 1 (74) is warmer, just 1 day later"],["Day 1 (74)","1","Day 2 (75) is warmer, 1 day later"],["Day 2 (75)","4","Day 3 (71), 4 (69), 5 (72) are all cooler; day 6 (76) is the first warmer day, 4 days later"],["Day 3 (71)","2","Day 5 (72) is the first warmer day, 2 days later"],["Day 4 (69)","1","Day 5 (72) is warmer, 1 day later"],["Day 5 (72)","1","Day 6 (76) is warmer, 1 day later"],["Day 6 (76)","0","Nothing later is warmer than 76"],["Day 7 (73, the last day)","0","Nothing exists after it"]]}

blocks.text: Recognizing this as "next greater element," but tracking DAY INDICES on the stack (instead of just values) directly, since the final answer needs an index DIFFERENCE, not the warmer value itself.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: This is structurally identical to finding the "next greater element" for every position, just returning a different piece of information (the index gap) once found.

Observation 2: Walking through the days left to right, maintaining a stack of DAY-INDICES still WAITING for a warmer day: whenever today's temperature is warmer than the temperature on the day at the stack's top index, that day's wait is resolved.

Observation 3: The resolved wait is simply TODAY'S index minus the WAITING day's index, since that is exactly how many days passed between them.

Observation 4: Repeating this pop-and-resolve while the stack's top day is still cooler correctly handles today resolving MULTIPLE waiting days at once.

Observation 5: Days remaining on the stack after the full scan never found a warmer day, so their answer stays 0 (the default).
This is the monotonic decreasing stack technique for "next greater element," storing indices so the final answer (a day-gap) is directly computable once each match is found.
For each day, scan forward through every later day until the first strictly warmer temperature is found, and record how many days that took.

items: For each day i, scan every later day j > i in order.
The first day j found with temps[j] > temps[i] gives the answer (j - i); if none is found, the answer stays 0.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The inner loop directly implements the definition: the FIRST later day with a strictly warmer temperature.
The result array defaults to all 0s, directly matching "no future warmer day" without needing a separate check.

blocks.text: Correctly finds each day's wait, since it directly scans exactly as the definition requires.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^2) in the worst case (for example, a strictly decreasing temperature sequence, where every scan reaches the very end).
Space: O(1) extra (excluding the output).
Limitation: repeating a forward scan for every day is wasteful; a single monotonic stack pass resolves ALL days' waits simultaneously.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rescans forward for every day independently. Instead, walk through temperatures ONCE, maintaining a monotonic decreasing stack of day-indices still waiting for warmth. Whenever today's temperature is warmer than the temperature at the stack's top index, pop and record today's index minus that index as the wait, repeating until the stack's top no longer qualifies.

Walk through temperatures with a stack of indices. For each index i: while the stack is non-empty and temps[stack top] < temps[i], pop that index and set its result to i minus that index. Push i. Indices remaining on the stack at the end keep their default answer of 0.
Use a monotonic decreasing stack of day-indices to resolve every day's wait in a single linear pass.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: Continuing this process through the rest of the array gives [1,1,4,2,1,1,0,0], matching the expected output.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each index is pushed and popped at most once.
Space: O(n), for the stack in the worst case.

Each index pushed onto the stack represents "a day still waiting to find a strictly warmer day further ahead." The moment such a day arrives, it is guaranteed to be the FIRST (nearest) warmer day for every cooler day currently sitting on top of the stack, since anything even warmer appearing earlier would have already resolved them. The resolved wait is simply the index difference, since that directly counts the number of days that passed.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Today is warmer than the temperature at the stack's top index","Pop and resolve (result = today's index - that index), possibly repeating for multiple cooler days below it"],["Today is not warmer than the top","Simply pushed, joining the \"waiting\" indices"],["Indices remain on the stack after the full scan","Those days never found a warmer day, keeping their default answer of 0"]]}

items: Storing INDICES (not temperatures) on the stack allows directly computing the day-gap (index difference) once a match is resolved.
The while loop's strict < comparison correctly matches the "strictly warmer" requirement (equal temperatures do NOT count as warmer).
The result array's default value of 0 directly matches the problem's specified default for "no future warmer day."

blocks.text: "Days until the next warmer value" is the "next greater element" pattern in disguise; storing INDICES (rather than values) on the monotonic stack directly enables computing the requested day-gap once each match is resolved.

items: Storing temperatures instead of indices on the stack, losing the ability to directly compute the day-gap once a match is found.
Using a non-strict comparison (<=) instead of strict (<), which would incorrectly treat an EQUAL temperature as "warmer."
Rescanning forward for each day individually, missing the opportunity to resolve all days in a single combined pass.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Strictly increasing temperatures","Every day (except the last) resolves immediately to a wait of 1"],["Strictly decreasing temperatures","Every day's answer stays 0, since nothing warmer ever appears later"],["All temperatures equal","Every day's answer stays 0, since the strict inequality never triggers"]]}

items: Explicitly connecting this problem to Next Greater Element I ("the SAME pattern, just returning a day-gap instead of a value") demonstrates strong pattern transfer and quickly clarifies the approach.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Number of days/positions until the next LARGER value" points directly to a monotonic decreasing stack, storing INDICES so the gap is directly computable.

items: How would you find the number of days until the next COOLER temperature instead? Use a monotonic INCREASING stack instead, popping while the top is warmer than today.
What is the amortized cost per element, and why? O(1) amortized, since each index is pushed exactly once and popped at most once across the entire algorithm.

How does this problem connect to Next Greater Element I and Next Greater Node In Linked List elsewhere in this category? All three share the exact same monotonic decreasing stack core technique, differing only in what information is ultimately extracted once a match is resolved (a value, a day-gap, or a linked-list value).

A direct application of the monotonic decreasing stack "next greater element" pattern from Next Greater Element I and Next Greater Node In Linked List elsewhere in this category, here extracting an index-gap rather than a value.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space.
Optimized (monotonic decreasing stack): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Monotonic decreasing stack for "next greater element" (indices, not values)
Core Idea: Track day-INDICES still waiting for warmth on the stack; a warmer day resolves every waiting cooler day's answer as the simple index difference
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Storing indices (not values) is what lets the resolved answer be computed directly as a day-gap once each match is found
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Monotonic decreasing stack of indices; a warmer day resolves result[idx] = today - idx for everything cooler waiting on top
